parole.significato: bagna cauda (dip made from anchovies, olive oil and garlic)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Piedmontese bagna càuda (literally “hot dip”). See also Italian bagna and caldo.
From the apocopic form of Bastiano, in turn an apheretic form of Sebastiano (“Sebastian”), or directly from Piedmontese Bastian, aphesis of Sebastian.

parole.significato: a person who deliberately contradicts someone else or the majority of people, usually out of spite or for the sake of i…
parole.testo: Literally, “contrary Sebastian”, possibly a direct borrowing from Piedmontese bastian contrari. The namesake of the expression is uncertain.

parole.significato: a traditional Piedmontese pudding prepared with cocoa and amaretti

parole.significato: a seat as a symbol of power
parole.testo: From Piedmontese or Lombard cadrega (“chair”), from Latin cathedra (“seat”), from Ancient Greek κᾰθέδρᾱ (kăthédrā, “chair of a teacher, throne”), whence also Italian cattedra, + -ino (diminutive suffix).
Borrowed from Piedmontese gàgno, from Latin gāneō (“glutton”).
Named after Gianduja, a Piedmontese stock character in the commedia dell'arte, in reference to its place of origin. From Piedmontese Giandoja (literally “John-o'-the-jug”).
Borrowed from Piedmontese grissin, ghërsin, diminutive of ghersa (“line, row”), which is ultimately from Latin cratis (“wickerwork, fascine”). Cognate with French gressin.

parole.significato: A title given to foreign (especially French) artists or high-ranking men during the 17th and 18th century.
parole.testo: Sense 2 is borrowed from Piedmontese monsù, while sense 3 is Neapolitan and Sicilian, all ultimately from French monsieur. Doublet of monsignore and messere.

parole.significato: a small, rectangular form of agnolotti
parole.testo: Borrowed from Piedmontese plin (“pinch, nip”), onomatopoeic, in reference to the gesture made to fold it.
